Eastern woodrats (Neotoma floridana) are medium-sized cricetid rodents widely distributed across the southeastern and south-central United States. Detailed life-history data for this species have been compiled from both field and captive studies. Neonates emerge from parturition weighing approximately 13.43 grams [Wwb = approximately 13.43 grams], a modest birth mass consistent with the altricial condition typical of the genus. This initial body mass is followed by a period of rapid growth during the suckling juvenile stage. The age at which nutritional independence is achieved, marked by the cessation of lactation, has been recorded at 22 days after birth [tx = 22 days after birth] under stable thermal conditions of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively short suckling period reflects the rapid developmental trajectory of Neotoma floridana, enabling young to transition to solid food and begin foraging independently at an early age compared to other rodents of similar adult body size.

Reproductive timing in Neotoma floridana follows a constrained schedule governed by physiological maturation. Gestation lasts approximately 33 days [tg = approximately 33 days] under the same core body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C] that characterizes this endothermic mammal. This gestation period is typical of temperate-zone cricetids and permits multiple litters within a single breeding season given appropriate environmental conditions. Following birth, the transition to reproductive maturity unfolds over the subsequent months. The time since birth at puberty, marking the onset of gametogenesis and the first potential for successful reproductive pairing, has been documented at 95 days after birth [tp = 95 days after birth] at 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This relatively delayed maturation relative to weaning (22 days) indicates a substantial period of juvenile growth and somatic development before the reproductive system becomes fully functional, a pattern that likely reduces the risk of early-life breeding failure.

Adult body size in Neotoma floridana is attained through a sigmoidal growth trajectory following the weaning transition. The ultimate wet weight, representing the asymptotic adult body mass achieved once skeletal and muscular growth are completed, has been recorded at 291 grams [Wwi = 291 grams] in well-nourished captive individuals. This maximum recorded body mass in adults places Neotoma floridana among the larger members of its genus, with males typically reaching slightly heavier masses than females, although the species exhibits considerable geographic variation. The wet weight at weaning, measured at 45.9 grams [Wwx = 45.9 grams], represents a substantial increase from the 13.43 gram [Wwb = 13.43 gram] neonatal mass, reflecting a more than threefold gain in mass during the three-week suckling period. The ratio of weaning mass to birth mass underscores the efficiency of maternal milk provisioning and the rapid growth rates characteristic of this species during early ontogeny.

Lifespan and reproductive output in Neotoma floridana reflect a life-history strategy oriented toward moderate iteroparity. Maximum recorded longevity in the wild, based on mark-recapture studies, reaches approximately 8.6 years [am = approximately 8.6 years] when individuals experience the typical body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. This lifespan is relatively extended for a rodent of its body mass and is consistent with patterns observed in other woodrat species that inhabit stable, resource-rich environments such as rock outcrops and hardwood forests. Under these same thermal conditions (37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]), females typically produce litters averaging 3.5 pups per litter [N_R_i = 3.5 pups per litter], a clutch size that is moderate among medium-sized cricetids. The combination of this moderate litter size with a relatively long reproductive lifespan allows Neotoma floridana to maintain stable population densities even in habitats where annual survivorship may be variable due to predation and environmental stochasticity.

The reproductive frequency of Neotoma floridana is tightly linked to seasonal resource availability and ambient conditions. In the southern portions of its range, breeding can extend from early spring through late autumn, with females capable of producing approximately 2.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 2.5 litters per year] when maintained at the typical body temperature of 37.5 °C [T = 37.5 °C]. When these two reproductive parameters are considered together, the resulting annual output—derived from 3.5 pups per litter and 2.5 litters annually—represents a moderate reproductive rate for a cricetid of this body size. Field studies indicate that this level of reproductive effort is sustainable because of the species' reliance on high-quality woody browse and mast crops, which provide the energetic resources necessary for both lactation and maternal body condition recovery between parturitions. Comparative data from congeneric species such as Neotoma mexicana suggest that the eastern woodrat's suite of life-history traits—moderate litter size, extended lifespan, and prolonged juvenile development period—aligns with a slow-to-moderate pace-of-life continuum typical of woodland-dwelling rodents.
